newsitem.title: FRANCE: France may hike some taxes to cut 1997 deficit.
newsitem.headline: France may hike some taxes to cut 1997 deficit.

text.p: France's Socialist-led government may tap corporations to fill an expected hole in this year's budget, a source close to the government said on Thursday.
The government is facing the delicate task of narrowing a big deficit to qualify for European monetary union while keeping an election campaign promise not to impose economic austerity.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's government is awaiting results of an audit of public finances due on Monday likely to show a deficit this year of about 3.6 percent of gross domestic product -- significantly higher than the three percent required by the Maastricht treaty on monetary union.
The government denied on Thursday that it had reached any conclusions about what to do about the budget gap.
"We have not made any decisions," government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann said.

Asked whether the government was considering a new austerity plan to bring down the deficit, Trautmann said, "No, it is out of the question." She said decisions on specific measures would be taken after the submission of the audit of public finances.
Jospin has said his government will take action to close the budget gap if needed but has ruled out new austerity just to meet a strict interpretation of Maastricht treaty criteria.
The government is expected to try to bring down the budget deficit by a few percentage points to around 3.3 percent of GDP to reach a level acceptable for monetary union.
A reduction of 0.3 percentage points in the deficit would imply finding new revenues or spending cuts of some 25 billion francs ($4.1 billion).

The government source said the government could raise corporate tax to around 40 percent of profits from its current level of 36.6 percent. A rise in employer social security contributions was also being studied.

Small- and medium-sized companies, seen as the country's engines of job creation, would be exempt from any corporate tax increase and it would be structured in such a way as to avoid harming investment, the source added.
The government could also raise taxes on savings for the well-off.

The source said proposed measures were concentrated on corporations and the wealthy because the government feared a heavy psychological impact that would slow economic growth if it were to enact measures affecting the broad middle class.
Jospin's government, in line with tradition, may also seek contributions from state-owned companies like savings bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations.
The government is also studying some savings measures.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn has been less precise about what the government would do, saying only that any measures to curb the budget deficit could affect companies and well-off households, and involve budget savings.
He has also said any measures affecting companies would be set up in such a way as to avoid damaging business investment.
Earlier, Education Minister Claude Allegre told French radio that the government would impose a one-off charge on profitable businesses to raise cash if needed.
"It's normal that those who make big profits in a difficult situation should contribute more than others. But there is no question of raising taxes," he said on RMC radio.
($ = 6.065 French Francs)
